passerby: Afternoon. Grand day for a walk, isn't it?
Morning! Say hello to everybody for me.
It's lovely up here this time of year. I never do get tired of it.
Afternoon — mind how you go, and enjoy the village.
trivia: Hobart was a near-empty Main Street until one antiquarian bookshop opened around 2000 — now there's a whole village of them.
East of Jefferson stands a real 13-sided barn, built in 1896, about sixty feet across — one of only two on the Register in this part of the state.
The Catskill Scenic Trail runs from Stamford to Hobart along an old railroad bed — a favorite walk and bike ride.
Mount Utsayantha, north of Stamford, is named for a princess in local legend — the lake below shares her name.
Route 23 becomes Main Street the moment it crosses into Stamford.
The Belvedere started out as a hotel, long before it became Stamford's hippest dive bar.
Stewart's keeps the local softball league's standings taped right to the ice cream case.
Tops is the only grocery store for a good half hour in any direction, which is worth remembering when you're out of milk.
Every June, Hobart's bookshops host three days of readings for the Festival of Women Writers.
Two coffee shops once opened in Stamford the very same week, neither one knowing the other existed.
Somehow there are an awful lot of people named Jess around here. Nobody's ever managed to count them all.
roadEnd: Not today. There's plenty to see back in town.
The road goes on, but the story's back this way.
That's as far as this week's story goes — might as well turn back.
Nothing more to find this way just yet. The village is waiting behind you.
holler: Hey! This isn't New York City — get out of the road!
You planning on standing there all day? Move it!
Road's for trucks, pal. Sidewalk's for people.
C'mon! Some of us have got places to be!
